clips.text_en_b1: An unbreakable rule of crypto has just broken. Rule 1 says breaking the 1D 200 SMA after a bear market starts the next bull run. Rule 2 is the 4-year cycle. If this bull run has begun, the bottom was 58k two months ago. That means the bear market was only 6 months long, when it should be about 12. These rules cannot both be right at this early stage. One of them is already failing. We are in uncharted territory now.
clips.source_hint: Biz thread says crypto's unbreakable rules are incompatible.
clips.text_en_b2: Two supposedly ironclad rules of the crypto market have just collapsed simultaneously. Rule one insists a confirmed break above the daily 200 SMA officially kicks off a bull run, yet the four-year cycle clearly has not elapsed. If we treat the recent 58k bottom as the cycle low, the bear market barely lasted six months instead of the usual twelve. Both principles simply cannot hold at this stage without one being outright wrong.
clips.text_en_c1: Two long-standing pillars of crypto market analysis have effectively collapsed overnight. The first axiom holds that a decisive breakout above the 200-day SMA signals the inception of a fresh bull cycle, while the second insists on the sacred four-year halving rhythm. If we are genuinely witnessing a new uptrend, then the recent floor at roughly 58k must be retroactively declared the bear market bottom. That would imply a mere six-month drawdown, an alarming departure from the customary twelve-month duration. Both frameworks cannot simultaneously hold water at such an embryonic stage, so one is destined to break.
clips.text_en_c2: Two seemingly immutable axioms of crypto markets have, in a single stroke, ceased to hold simultaneously. The first, that a decisive breach of the daily 200 SMA following a protracted bear market heralds the onset of a fresh bull cycle, now appears to have been satisfied; the second, the hallowed four-year rhythm traced back to Bitcoin's earliest epochs, emphatically has not. Should the present rally indeed constitute the new uptrend, then capitulation occurred at roughly 58k a mere two months back, implying a downturn of barely six months rather than the customary twelve. Both propositions, plainly, cannot remain valid at this juncture; one must already be buckling. Participants who have wagered their portfolios on an uninterrupted ascent are, quite understandably, unlikely to find much rest tonight.

After the company reported only modest second-quarter revenue growth, he admitted he had misjudged the speed at which AI would reshape the economy. He pointed to the difficulty companies and individuals have in changing established habits. The Wall Street Journal reported OpenAI generated $6.7 billion in revenue last quarter.

clips.text_en_c1: Sam Altman has finally conceded what skeptics have long suspected: the projected AI takeover timeline is slipping considerably because ordinary humans stubbornly refuse to integrate the technology into their workflows. Following OpenAI's rather underwhelming second-quarter revenue report, the CEO candidly acknowledged that he had fundamentally misjudged the velocity at which artificial intelligence would permeate and reshape the broader economy. He attributed the friction to deeply ingrained corporate habits and individual inertia, forces that no amount of venture capital can simply wish away. clips.text_en_c2: Sam Altman has, in a rare concession, publicly conceded that his projected timeline for the AI takeover has slipped considerably, owing primarily to humanity's entrenched reluctance to integrate these tools into daily workflows. Following OpenAI's disclosure of merely modest revenue growth in the second quarter, the CEO acknowledged that he had substantially overestimated the velocity with which artificial intelligence would restructure the economic landscape, citing the formidable difficulty companies and individuals encounter when attempting to dislodge long-established habits. According to reporting in the Wall Street Journal, OpenAI generated some $6.7 billion in revenue during that quarter. Whether this represents genuine reprieve for the gainfully employed, or merely a slower-dawning obsolescence, remains, for the moment, an open question.

clips.text_zh: 有個兄弟5x5做咗3年，每週先gym一次，bench得1RM 90kg。佢188cm 87kg喎。咁我每週三次應該快過佢？唔知 肥仔信今日又叫我去gym 🙏 好似要認真諗下個programme
clips.text_en_b1: Is strength really the best way to train? I have been following a simple 5x5 routine for 3 years. I gym once per week, yes, little bitch levels of frequency. I alternate bench press, squats, and deadlifts each week, then repeat. After 3 years of 5x5 at 80 percent of my 1RM, I can barely do a decent amount. I am 27, 188cm, 87kg. My bench 1RM is only 90kg. What am I doing wrong?
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread asking if strength training is actually best.
clips.text_en_b2: Strength training might not be the magic bullet everyone claims it is, at least not at this frequency. I have stuck to a basic 5x5 programme for three solid years while only managing a single weekly gym session, rotating between bench, squats, and deadlifts. Working at roughly 80 percent of my one-rep max, my bench 1RM has crawled up to a measly 90kg despite being 188cm and 87kg at age 27.
clips.text_en_c1: Three years of disciplined 5x5 training and the returns are frankly underwhelming. I have been rotating bench press, squats, and deadlifts on alternating weeks, training exactly once per week because life evidently refuses to accommodate additional gym visits. Despite religiously adhering to eighty percent of my one-rep max, my physique remains stubbornly mediocre by any objective standard. The numbers paint an unflattering portrait: I am 27 years old, 188 centimetres tall, and weigh 87 kilograms, yet my bench press one-rep max languishes at a measly 90 kilograms. Surely a comparable individual training three times weekly would progress substantially faster.
clips.text_en_c2: There exists a brother, by his own account a devoted adherent of the venerable 5x5 programme for the past three years, who trains but once weekly and has nevertheless laboured to coax a meagre bench-press 1RM of 90kg from his considerable 188cm, 87kg frame. He rotates bench, squat, and deadlift on successive weeks, executing each session at roughly 80 percent of his one-rep maximum, then repeats the cycle ad infinitum. The returns, after thirty-six months of such Spartan devotion, are, to put it charitably, underwhelming. By the elementary arithmetic of training frequency alone, thrice-weekly sessions ought to yield disproportionately superior progress, though the intervening variable of programme design cannot, of course, be discounted.

clips.text_en_b1: The Big O. Anyone remember this anime? It is pretty cool. If you ever wondered what it would be like if Batman did not suck, then this is what you should watch. It has that same dark detective noir style, giant mechs, and a great jazz soundtrack. The show originally aired in 1999 but still holds up today. Give it a try if you have not seen it.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread recommending classic mecha noir anime The Big O.
clips.text_en_b2: The Big O has finally surfaced in a thread after years of silence, so now seems like the perfect moment to revisit it. Essentially, picture Batman if he had been written competently, blending noir detective atmosphere with towering mechs and a genuinely phenomenal jazz soundtrack that still holds up remarkably well. Although my usual rotation leans toward Gundam 00 and Demon Slayer, this 1999 classic absolutely deserves another watch tonight.
clips.text_en_c1: A fellow enthusiast finally broached the subject, and the nostalgia hit like a freight train. The Big O deserves far more recognition than it typically receives, a criminally underrated gem that originally aired in 1999 yet retains an extraordinary capacity to captivate modern audiences. Picture Batman stripped of his more egregious narrative excesses and grafted onto a neo-noir Paradigm City backdrop, then amplified through colossal mechs and a genuinely sublime jazz-infused soundtrack that would make Cowboy Bebop envious. While my own viewing habits lean heavily toward Gundam 00 and Demon Slayer, this particular series occupies a singular niche that warrants immediate queuing upon returning home tonight.
clips.text_en_c2: The Big O, a title that has hovered in the penumbra of anime discourse for the better part of two decades, has at last surfaced in conversation, prompting an almost Proustian swell of nostalgia. For those who have long entertained the heretical thought that Batman, were he stripped of his more ponderous excesses, might actually constitute compelling viewing, this 1999 series offers a compelling rejoinder: a noir-inflected detective aesthetic married to towering mecha and underscored by a jazz soundtrack of considerable sophistication. Although my own recent viewing has skewed toward Gundam 00 and Demon Slayer, the occasion warrants queueing up an episode upon returning home this evening, if only to verify whether memory has been unduly kind.
